by Daryl Ducharme, Open Source Programs Office

A look around the world of open source

Automated tools are flooding open source repositories with bug reports and pull requests faster than human maintainers can review patches, coordinate security embargoes, or fund the work behind critical infrastructure. Across this edition, we trace how builders are responding—replacing brute-force diff skimming with codified invariants, protecting newcomer on-ramps and neutral foundation governance instead of reactionary gatekeeping, and designing open social protocols that keep control with people rather than closed platforms.

Upcoming events

🗓️ December 2026

  • Yocto Project Virtual Summit 2026.12 (December 1–3, 2026) – Virtual. Community summit for embedded Linux engineers and maintainers building custom, reproducible Linux distributions across edge and Internet of Things (IoT) hardware.
  • Open Source Summit Japan 2026 (December 7–9, 2026) – Tokyo, Japan. The Linux Foundation's premier Asia-Pacific conference connecting open source developers, kernel maintainers, and enterprise leaders across cloud, embedded Linux, and open source AI—featuring a keynote by Google's Kaz Sato on building agents on open standards alongside sessions from Googlers Tanya Sharma and Tarun Sahu.
  • Open Compliance Summit 2026 (December 10–11, 2026) – Tokyo, Japan. Specialized gathering uniting legal, security, and Open Source Programs Office (OSPO) practitioners around OpenChain, Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX), software bills of materials (SBOMs), and global open source supply-chain compliance.

🗓️ January 2027

  • Free and Open Source Software Developers' European Meeting (FOSDEM) 2027 (January 30–31, 2027) – Brussels, Belgium. Europe's largest free, volunteer-organized gathering for free and open source software developers at the Université libre de Bruxelles, with individual developer room calls for participation closing through early December.

🗓️ February 2027

  • Academy Software Foundation (ASWF) Open Source Forum (February 18, 2027) – Los Angeles, California, USA. Annual forum bringing engineering and studio leaders together on open source tooling for animation, visual effects, and digital media production.
  • The Linux Foundation Member Summit 2027 (February 22–23, 2027) – Half Moon Bay, California, USA. Annual strategy and governance gathering for Linux Foundation member organizations and project boards across foundational open source ecosystems.

Open calls for proposals (CFPs)

  • FOSDEM 2027 Community Developer Rooms (Event: January 30–31, 2027 – Brussels, Belgium) – Developer room CFP deadlines: November 20 – December 3, 2026 (rolling deadlines across 77 accepted developer rooms, with schedules published December 7).
  • AtmosphereConf 2027 (Event: April 29 – May 2, 2027 – Amsterdam, The Netherlands) – Round 1 CFP deadline: November 30, 2026 (Round 2 opens January 11, 2027). Community conference uniting developers and researchers building on the Authenticated Transfer Protocol (AT Protocol) across Build, Create, Inform, and Govern tracks.
  • NeoCloudCon Europe 2027 (KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe Co-Located Event) (Event: March 15, 2027 – Barcelona, Spain) – CFP deadline: November 30, 2026, at 23:59 Central European Time (CET). Co-located Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) summit on AI cloud platforms, GPU orchestration, and open distributed infrastructure.
  • CNCF Maintainer Summit Europe 2027 (Event: March 14, 2027 – Barcelona, Spain) – CFP deadline: December 1, 2026 (23:59 CET). Exclusive summit for CNCF project maintainers, Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) members, and Technical Advisory Group (TAG) leads focused on governance, API design, and project health.
  • Academy Software Foundation (ASWF) Open Source Forum 2027 (Event: February 18, 2027 – Los Angeles, California, USA) – CFP deadline: December 6, 2026, at 11:59 PM Pacific Time (PT). Invites technical proposals on new technologies impacting studios across AI and machine learning, virtual production, pipeline tooling, computer graphics, and immersive films.
  • PyCon US 2027 (Event: May 12–18, 2027 – Long Beach, California, USA) – CFP deadline: December 19, 2026 (Proposal Mentorship Program deadline: November 27). Flagship community conference for the Python programming language inviting talks, Charlas, tutorials, and posters.

Open source reads and links

  • [Article] ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story - Automated scanners like Microsoft's Multi-Model Agentic Scanning Harness (MDASH) found 59 Linux kernel bugs, yet turning findings into reports still took over four person-months—while half of memory-management reviewer Lorenzo Stoakes's queue turned into AI noise. With Linus Torvalds spotting early AI fixes in Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF), can automated remediation truly catch up to human reviewer burnout?
  • [Article] Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.” - When leaked identifiers and live honeypot probing collided with critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities across 68.8% of identified websites, Chainguard shipped patched containers six hours ahead of embargo. As AI disassembly shrinks exploit timelines faster than ecosystem packaging, how should maintainers and distributors agree ahead of time when an emergency breaks an embargo?
  • [Article] Open-source security in the AI exploit era: Patch without changing a thing - With disclosure-to-exploit windows down to one day and 18 million npm packages resting on single maintainers, enterprises can no longer treat open source as free infrastructure. Routing builds through commercial pre-patched dependency proxies sounds convenient, yet how can this model support upstream maintainers' livelihoods rather than drain community sustainability?
  • [Article] A step-by-step guide for how to kill the line-by-line code review - "Agents verify; people decide" captures a compelling review skeleton: turning recurring pull-request feedback into deterministic, scope-bounded checks while letting maintainers review session intent, core decisions, and runtime evidence. How could open source teams implement invariant-driven verification across GitHub, Tangled, or self-hosted forges without fossilizing stale rules?
  • [Article] Container builds on Kubernetes, and why bots shouldn’t get good first issues - Stepping from OpenShift into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox taught Shipwright maintainer Adam Kaplan what neutral governance unlocks for container builds on Kubernetes. His warning on AI contribution habits deserves wider debate: if bots clear every "good first issue," where do tomorrow's human maintainers learn to contribute?
  • [Article] r/opensource just banned AI, non-English speakers, and more - Moderators of Reddit’s r/opensource subreddit banned any project using or built for AI, required projects to be at least a year old with three or more contributors, and barred non-English speakers because moderators say they cannot separate AI-written text from machine translation. Where is the line between stopping automated spam and shutting out solo developers and international contributors?
  • [Article] Five years after the fork, OpenSearch is slowly stepping out of AWS’s shadow - Two years after joining the Linux Foundation, Amazon Web Services (AWS) dropped from 91% to 72% of OpenSearch contributions while self-managed deployments jumped from 37% to 60%—yet 24% of surveyed non-adopters still cite vendor dominance. Beyond legal license independence, what sustained stewardship actually convinces communities a corporate fork is truly neutral?
  • [Essay] ATProto is a better IndieWeb - Measuring the Authenticated Transfer Protocol (AT Protocol) against five IndieWeb values—permanence, pluralism, interoperability, sovereignty, and agency—The Paper Pilot argues decoupled Personal Data Servers (PDSes) and shared Lexicons unlock richer software diversity than optional microformats, especially alongside Standard.site. When lowering onboarding barriers competes with self-hosting, where should protocols draw the line?
  • [Proposal] A proposal for opening AT URIs - Over 20% of links saved to Semble now expose AT Protocol metadata, yet clicking an at:// Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) still traps apps into hardcoding "open in Bluesky." By proposing community.lexicon.app preference records without bloating PDSes, how can Open Social Web apps give readers true default-client choice?

Which of these stories will you be chatting about at your next meetup or conference? Let us know! Share with us on our @GoogleOSS X account or our @opensource.google Bluesky account.
